documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is one of the major technological advancements of this century, bearing incredible potential for users through AI-powered applications and tools in numerous domains. Being often black-box (i.e., its decision-making process is unintelligible), developers typically resort to eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to interpret the behavior of AI models to produce systems that are transparent, fair, reliable, and trustworthy. However, presenting explanations to the user is not trivial and is often left as a secondary aspect of the system’s design process, leading to AI systems that are not useful to end-users. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review on Explanation User Interfaces (XUIs) to gain a deeper understanding of the solutions and design guidelines employed in the academic literature to effectively present explanations to users. To improve the contribution and real-world impact of this survey, we also present a platform to support Human-cEnteRed developMent of Explainable user interfaceS (HERMES) and guide practitioners and scholars in the design and evaluation of XUIs.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

Abstract Drawing on the notion of workplace learning this study examines how academic development can design and facilitate team learning in the academic workplace to support co-constructive educational innovation. Based on a qualitative case study at a Swiss University of Teacher Education, it analyses a participatory initiative addressing generative artificial intelligence (genAI) in assessment. The staged process combined SWOT-based collective sense-making, a design sprint, selective project funding, and facilitated reflection during project development. Data consisted of process documentation and collaboratively generated written reflections, which were analysed and refined through iterative feedback and co-writing. The findings show how structured formats, shared artefacts, and deliberate facilitation enabled participants to make distributed expertise visible, develop shared problem understandings, form project teams, and move from exchange towards co-construction and coordinated experimentation. At the same time, public pitching, funding decisions, time pressures, and institutional constraints created tensions between collaboration and competition, openness and focus, and participation and decision-making. The study suggests that academic development can support educational innovation by acting as facilitator, trust-building broker, and co-learner. Its contribution lies in conceptualising participatory innovation processes as workplace-learning arrangements that connect emerging team-learning processes with local experimentation and wider institutional conversations, while recognising that organisational learning requires further institutional uptake.

Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.

The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

Rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into enterprise processes highlights critical gaps in workforce readiness in terms of skills required for successful implementation of new technologies. This paper introduces a framework which will enable use of generative AI for conducting dynamic skill gap analysis and providing personalized recommendations for upskilling. The framework includes mapping of competencies according to shifting role demands, individual performance assessment through AI and adaptation of learning path for each individual based on results. Using the information obtained from surveys about AI adoption in enterprises and competency maps developed in recent research, this paper will show how generative AI can be used for making static learning programs adaptive and relevant to the current needs of learners. The problem discussed in the paper is related to not only technical AI literacy, but also to human skills, such as critical thinking, ethical decision-making and change management. Comparative analysis of methods shows that personalized training offered by generative AI is more engaging and relevant than generic models of training programs.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new possibilities for distance education through conversational learning support, personalised explanations, automated feedback and multilingual assistance. However, its integration also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, unequal access, information reliability, learner autonomy and data privacy. This paper develops a conceptual framework for integrating GenAI into distance education through a human-in-the-loop approach. Drawing on relevant scholarly literature and international educational policy documents, the study examines the relationship between AI-supported personalisation, inclusive learning, human oversight and academic accountability. It proposes an integrated framework in which teachers and learners retain meaningful decision-making authority while AI provides supplementary educational support. The framework comprises five dimensions: human agency, equitable access, learner-centred personalisation, academic integrity and responsible data governance. The paper argues that technological availability alone cannot guarantee educational improvement; effective implementation also requires AI literacy, appropriate assessment practices, institutional policies and continuous human evaluation. The proposed framework offers conceptual guidance for higher-education institutions seeking to adopt GenAI responsibly in distance-learning environments. As a conceptual contribution, it requires subsequent empirical evaluation to establish its applicability across different educational contexts.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping digital marketing by enabling personalised, scalable, and innovative content, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding authenticity and consumer trust. This study examines how Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Personalization, and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation influence Brand Perception and Purchase Intention among Generation Z consumers, with Brand Perception serving as a mediating mechanism. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using data from 425 Generation Z consumers collected through a structured questionnaire based on five-point Likert-type scales. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson and Spearman correlations, multiple regression, variance inflation factors, HC3 robust standard errors, and bootstrapped mediation analysis based on 5,000 resamples. The findings indicate that Perceived Authenticity (β = .234), Perceived Personalization (β = .160), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .407) significantly and positively influence Brand Perception. Brand Perception significantly predicts Purchase Intention (β = .520). Significant indirect effects were observed for Perceived Authenticity (β = .122), Perceived Personalization (β = .083), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .212) through Brand Perception. The findings demonstrate that consumer responses to GenAI marketing translate into purchase intention substantially through broader brand evaluations. The study highlights the importance of combining AI-enabled innovation and personalization with authenticity and consistent brand positioning.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p < .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p < .001) and PU (β = .218, p < .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p < .001) and SRL (β = .202, p < .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce the time and cognitive effort required for university learning, yet technical efficiency does not necessarily translate into improved student well-being. This article develops and tests a conversion account of this paradox by distinguishing efficiency gains that remain available as student-controlled resources from gains that are associated with perceived increases in performance expectations, competitive pressure, verification work, and dependence. A sequential three-study mixed-methods program was conducted with undergraduates in Jiangxi Province. Study 1 used codebook thematic analysis of 42 interviews to identify six mechanisms linking immediate efficiency to resource retention or perceived pressure. Study 2 surveyed 1268 students across eight universities. GenAI use was strongly associated with perceived efficiency gains, but also with perceived performance-standard escalation and verification burden. Positive retention and negative competition pathways were similar in magnitude, yielding a nonsignificant total association with well-being; working-time retention strengthened the efficiency–well-being association. Because Study 2 was cross-sectional, these pathways are interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Study 3 used a 2 × 2 experiment (N = 320) and found that AI access improved task quality and reduced completion time under both performance-norm conditions, whereas gains in autonomy, retained time, and state well-being were evident under the stable norm but not statistically distinguishable from zero under the escalated norm. The findings distinguish technical affordance from context-dependent conversion and suggest that responsible AI integration should consider whether efficiency gains remain available for learning, recovery, and student-directed use alongside productivity.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. They also reported significantly higher overall SRL and greater use of SRL strategies. No significant differences were found in general motivation, SRL motivation, SRL planning and organization, or self-efficacy. The AI-guided group showed significantly lower raw variability in satisfaction and self-efficacy. However, a sensitivity analysis did not establish that these variance differences remained after accounting for mean-related constraints on the bounded response scale. The findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a scaffold for error analysis when integrated in ways that maintain students’ active cognitive engagement.

documents.abstract: This project documents the methods and analytical framework of a scoping review examining how generative artificial intelligence is used to support learning and research competency development among postgraduate nursing students. The review focuses on six competency domains: information literacy and evidence retrieval, evidence-based practice competency, research methodology and analytical skills, academic writing and scientific communication, critical thinking and research thinking, and AI literacy and responsible AI use. Study selection and data charting were completed before OSF registration; therefore, the registration is intended to provide a transparent record of the review methods rather than a prospective preregistration.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, influencing how students learn, produce knowledge, and engage in assessments. This study examines the ethical implications of AI integration in university courses and its perceived impact on students’ cognitive skills. Using a mixed-methods secondary data analysis, survey data from 23,218 students across 109 countries and 252 teachers from China, Romania, India, and Brunei were analyzed to explore perceptions of AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, behavioral intentions, and cognitive outcomes. The results have shown that although students are aware of the potential of AI in improving the efficiency and content creation and assistance in the learning process, there are still concerns about overdependence, plagiarism, and lack of critical thinking. The views of faculty underline moral direction and the necessity of systematic assimilation. Developing upon these insights, a theoretical framework is developed that connects antecedent variables, behavior intentions and institutional context to two outcomes the cognitive impact and institutional influence. This framework offers a guide on how universities should introduce generative AI in a responsible manner, and strike a balance between ethical principles and training higher-order cognitive abilities.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to innovation in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet resource constraints limit their ability to exploit it. Governments worldwide provide institutional support to encourage SME AI adoption, but whether such support translates into innovation depends on internal organizational conditions that remain poorly understood. Drawing on institutional theory, this study treats government support as a source of coercive, normative, and mimetic pressure and develops an integrative conceptual model in which it influences SME innovation performance through AI adoption intensity, with organizational learning capability as a mediator and organizational readiness as a moderator. The model specifies that government support raises adoption intensity, which in turn enhances innovation performance; that organizational learning capability partially mediates this effect; and that organizational readiness strengthens the link between government support and adoption intensity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design is proposed: structured questionnaires will collect no fewer than 200 valid responses from SMEs, analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Theoretically, the study is expected to extend institutional theory from the adoption/non-adoption dichotomy to a continuous adoption-intensity construct and to position organizational learning as the channel transmitting adoption into innovation. Practically, it can inform the design of differentiated government policy and SME capability building.

We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into environmental sustainability strategies presents a critical dilemma known as the "Green Tech Paradox." While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to optimize resource allocation, predict climate patterns, and enhance energy efficiency across industrial sectors, its deployment carries substantial, often overlooked, ecological costs. This research provides a critical analysis of the dual role AI plays as both a catalyst for eco-innovations and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. On the positive frontier, AI-driven applications accelerate sustainability by enabling smart power grids, improving carbon capture systems, facilitating precision agriculture, and modeling complex environmental crises. Machine learning algorithms enhance operational efficiency, reducing waste and carbon footprints in manufacturing and logistics. However, these beneficial outcomes are counterbalanced by the escalating physical footprint of AI infrastructure. The training and continuous execution of complex neural networks demand massive amounts of electricity, heavily relying on fossil-fuel-dominant energy grids. Furthermore, data centers consume millions of liters of freshwater daily for cooling mechanisms, accelerating localized water scarcity, while the rapid obsolescence of specialized hardware generates growing volumes of hazardous electronic waste. This paper evaluates this structural tension through a multidimensional synthesis of secondary data, life-cycle assessments, and resource consumption metrics across global data centers. The analysis reveals that without stringent regulatory frameworks and sustainable design interventions, the environmental degradation caused by AI's hardware lifecycle risks surpassing its ecological benefits. Ultimately, the study advocates for a paradigm shift toward "Green AI"—prioritizing algorithmic efficiency, renewable energy integration for computing infrastructure, sustainable hardware lifecycle management, and policy-driven eco-design standards. By establishing transparent auditing protocols, researchers and industry leaders can mitigate the hidden ecological liabilities of artificial intelligence, ensuring that modern technological advancement aligns genuinely with global net-zero targets and long-term planetary boundaries. Keywords: Green AI, Climate change mitigation, Sustainable development goals (SDGs), Environmental governance, Lifecycle assessment of AI.

Objectives: This study comprehensively investigates the underlying mechanisms through which green transformational leadership and work motivation influence sustainable employee performance. Specifically, the research evaluates the pivotal mediating role of employee engagement within the highly analytical and bureaucratic environment of Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank. Methodology: We employed an explanatory quantitative research design utilizing a cross-sectional survey approach. The empirical data were collected from a carefully determined sample of 158 permanent employees across four strategic departments at Bank Indonesia using a stratified random sampling approach. To test the complex structural relationships and mediation effects, we applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using the SmartPLS 4 software, executing a rigorous bootstrapping procedure with 5,000 subsamples. Finding: The empirical analysis reveals a compelling theoretical anomaly where green transformational leadership does not directly drive sustainable employee performance. Conversely, intrinsic work motivation exerts a strong, positive, and direct impact on the sustainability of employee performance. More importantly, both green leadership and work motivation are highly effective in cultivating deep employee engagement. Consequently, employee engagement emerges as a significant driver of sustainable performance, acting as a full mediator for green transformational leadership and a partial mediator for work motivation. Conclusion: Employee engagement functions as an absolute psychological bridge in a central banking context. Without this deep emotional and cognitive involvement, top-down environmental leadership visions and latent intrinsic motivation cannot effectively materialize into resilient, long-term sustainable performance.

We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for UI/UX evaluation and design decision support; however, their responses are often generated as implicit and unstructured outputs, making cognitive processes and judgment rationale difficult to trace. Moreover, the quality of LLM-based judgments may vary depending on users’ prompting proficiency, limiting the consistency of AI-assisted evaluation. This study proposes HIPA (Human Information Processing Architecture), a cognitive response architecture that structures LLM outputs based on the human information processing (HIP) model and investigates the manifestation of human cognitive stages in conventional LLM responses. HIPA maps four HIP stages—perception, working memory, decision making, and response execution—into a two-stage response structure consisting of information provision and judgment support through knowledge-grounded prompting with GPT-4o. An exploratory evaluation was conducted with seven participants with different prompting proficiency levels who assessed the same mobile login interface using a general LLM. Responses were coded according to HIP-stage manifestation using a three-point scale. The results showed that perception and response execution were consistently observed, whereas working memory and decision-making stages varied depending on prompt systematicity. These findings indicate that general LLM responses do not inherently provide cognitively structured judgment support. HIPA provides a human-centered framework for developing AI-assisted UI/UX evaluation systems based on human cognitive principles.

Human factors and ergonomics (HFE) is vital for optimising human-centred system design. This study aimed to synthesise research on HFE and examine its historical evolution, current landscape and emerging trends. A bibliometric analysis and a knowledge-domain mapping analysis were conducted to combine perspectives on journal development and article output. This study focused on 24 journals classified in the ergonomics category in the Journal Citation Reports of 2024. Critical information for the 24 HFE journals was investigated, including commencement year of publication, composition of editorial boards, number of published papers, publishing models, 2024 quartile rankings and impact factors and 5-year impact factors. Two visualisation tools, VOSviewer and CiteSpace, were used to perform the bibliometric analysis of the 26,026 HFE documents in the Web of Science Core Collection, spanning 2010 to 2024. Results showed that HFE literature has evolved from classical industrial origins to modern technological paradigms. Increased collaborations across different research areas to address HFE problems were observed. The review also identified key domain expansions across high-impact emerging HFE frontiers, including artificial intelligence, extended reality, autonomous vehicles and wearable technologies. Building upon these findings, the study may provide in-depth insights into the critical future HFE research directions.

documents.abstract: BackgroundAutomation, including both robots and AI, are increasingly implemented in the public sector to handle an increased demand for services while facing a shortage of staff. However, little is known of how automation is related to employees' work characteristics and well-being.ObjectiveThe purpose of the present study was to examine how automation is related to work characteristics and well-being in a national sample of social workers.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted with a sample of 1428 social workers in Sweden, comparing those working with automation technologies (e.g., robotization in terms of automated decision-making support in financial aid) to those without.ResultsThe findings indicate that automation is negatively related to relational aspects of work, such as beneficiary contact and social support, and increases perceived workload and role conflict. However, no significant differences were found on decision-making autonomy, role clarity, or skill variety. Despite these work design changes, no significant differences in well-being outcomes, such as burnout and vigor, were observed between the two groups.ConclusionThe findings suggest that automation may alter the nature of social work without necessarily changing employee well-being. These insights have implications for organizations seeking to implement automation in a way that supports employees' work experience and well-being.

The purpose of the research -This article examines human capital assessment through the integration of heterogeneous data and artificial intelligence in the context of the digital economy.The study aims to identify the interrelationships among artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and human capital, and to empirically evaluate how these factors influence productivity. Research methodology -The research applies analysis, comparison, systematization, grouping, and generalization methods.Its empirical part is based on panel data covering the period 2010-2024 and obtained from open international statistical databases.The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, unit root tests, cointegration analysis, multivariate regression modeling, and Granger causality testing.This methodological approach allows a comprehensive assessment of the interaction between artificial intelligence, digital transformation, human capital, and productivity.Results of the research -The findings show that artificial intelligence has a significant positive impact on productivity, while human capital strongly reinforces this effect.Digital transformation also contributes positively through better data processing and resource allocation.The results confirm long-run relationships among the variables and identify artificial intelligence and human capital as major drivers of productivity growth.Originality and scientific novelty of the research -The study offers an integrated and multidimensional framework for evaluating human capital in the digital economy.

This article presents a systematic literature review of the role of human capital in digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on how these developments reshape workforce competencies and human resource management (HRM) during the transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the study combines thematic coding with comparative analysis. From an initial pool of 216 publications, 46 studies were selected for in-depth analysis. The review examines how AI and digitalisation change workforce skill requirements and how HRM mechanisms can help organisations develop and sustain the necessary competencies. The findings indicate a shift from routine and manual tasks toward hybrid competency profiles that integrate data analytics skills, AI literacy, human–machine interaction skills, and higher-order socio-cognitive capabilities, including adaptive reasoning, collaboration, and ethical judgement. HRM emerges as a strategic integrator that supports continuous reskilling, predictive skills-gap analysis, and the development of effective human–AI teams. Based on these findings, the study proposes a multilevel framework explaining how institutional mechanisms, organisational strategy, HRM practices, and human–AI complementarity jointly shape workforce competitiveness in AI-enabled digital transformation. The framework contributes to human-centric digitalisation by linking workforce competitiveness to capability velocity and human–AI complementarity. It also provides managerial implications for designing learning, governance, and decision-making structures that enable organisations to respond to evolving competency requirements and translate technological potential into sustainable operational advantages.

Service organizations increasingly employ artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to allocate financial, technological, workforce, and operational resources. Although algorithmic systems can process complex organizational data, purely prediction-driven approaches may generate recommendations that are difficult for managers to interpret, validate, or reconcile with organizational constraints. These limitations become particularly important in healthcare and other information-intensive service environments where resource allocation decisions interact with workforce capacity, digital workflows, privacy requirements, project priorities, and service quality objectives. This study proposes a human centered explainable artificial intelligence framework for adaptive resource allocation and decision governance. The framework integrates predictive modeling, multi objective optimization, and explainability mechanisms within a structured decision support architecture. Rather than optimizing a single performance measure, the proposed approach considers multiple objectives including operational efficiency, resource utilization, service responsiveness, workforce capacity, fairness, and decision transparency. A human-in-the-loop governance mechanism allows decision-makers to review explanations, modify organizational constraints, and evaluate alternative allocation scenarios before recommendations are implemented. Because real organizational data are not used in the present study, the framework is evaluated using synthetically generated operational environments representing variations in demand, workforce availability, resource limitations, project priorities, and unexpected disruptions. Scenario and sensitivity analyses can then examine how resource allocation recommendations change under alternative organizational conditions. The principal contribution is an integrated analytical architecture in which optimization and explainability operate as complementary components of organizational decision making. The proposed framework can provide a foundation for transparent resource allocation systems applicable to healthcare, professional services, digital enterprises, and other service-oriented organizations seeking to improve efficiency and resilience while retaining managerial oversight.

documents.abstract: Hybrid work has moved from an emergency response to a deliberate work-design option, but its productivity consequences depend on how flexibility and digital coordination are organized. This study examined the relationship between hybrid work model and employee productivity in civil society organizations in Nigeria. Specifically, it assessed the relationship between work-location flexibility and employee productivity and determined the relationship between digital collaboration effectiveness and employee productivity. A survey research design was adopted. The study covered eight selected civil society organizations, with a population of 267 employees whose roles were compatible with hybrid work. A sample of 160 employees was selected, 155 questionnaires were returned and 152 usable responses were analyzed. Work-location flexibility and digital collaboration effectiveness were used as dimensions of the hybrid work model, while employee productivity was measured through task completion, output quality, timeliness, target attainment and work efficiency. The coded questionnaire data were analysed in EViews 10.0, where descriptive statistics were computed and the multiple regression model was estimated at the 5% significance level. The findings showed that work-location flexibility had a significant positive relationship with employee productivity (Coeff. = 0.3881; p-value = 0.0000), while digital collaboration effectiveness also had a significant positive relationship with employee productivity (Coeff. = 0.4552; p value = 0.0000). The model explained approximately 58.5% of the variation in employee productivity. The study concluded that hybrid work improves productivity in civil society organizations when location flexibility is accompanied by reliable digital collaboration, clear work routines and outcome-focused accountability. It recommended that civil society organizations formalize role-based hybrid schedules and strengthen the digital collaboration systems through which distributed employees coordinate tasks, share documents, monitor deadlines and maintain team visibility.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) is characterised by the convergence of new technologies encompassing artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT), and these innovations have permeated the everyday lives of young people globally, including in Nigeria. This study explored the level and factors of ICT engagement and knowledge acquisition among undergraduate students in Lagos State University (LASU). A descriptive survey design was adopted. Quantitative data was collected from 1,009 undergraduate students in the Faculties of Science and Social Sciences through an online questionnaire which was distributed through social media platforms, and the data collection spanned three weeks. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies and percentages) with IBM SPSS Statistics version 26. The findings revealed a high level of ICT engagement in academic activities: most respondents actively used digital devices for academic purposes, expressed confidence in using diverse ICT tools, and participated in online discussions and forums. The primary channels of knowledge acquisition combined traditional sources, notably lecture notes and print textbooks, with digital resources such as educational websites, e-books and online databases, while reliance on the university library showed signs of decline. Respondents overwhelmingly perceived that ICT engagement enhances their understanding of course content, broadens their knowledge beyond classroom instruction and contributes to critical thinking skills. The study recommends comprehensive digital literacy programmes, equitable ICT infrastructure and the modernisation of library services to consolidate these gains

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed the capacity of organisations to deliver personalised recommendations, communications, customer service and digital experiences at scale. This study develops and empirically tests a comprehensive model linking AI-based personalisation with customer loyalty through the mechanisms of trust and customer satisfaction, while simultaneously examining AI service quality and privacy concern as contextual factors. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 400 digital-service users through a structured 5-point Likert-scale questionnaire. The analysis encompasses descriptive statistics, reliability testing, KMO and Bartlett's tests, correlation analysis, multiple regression, mediation and moderation analysis, and selected demographic tests. The results demonstrate acceptable internal consistency for all constructs, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from .801 to .865. The KMO value was .916 and Bartlett's test was statistically significant, indicating that the item correlation matrix was suitable for factor-oriented analysis. AI-based personalisation exhibited a positive association with customer loyalty (β = .380, p < .001), explaining 14.4% of its variance in the simple regression. The full regression model explained 42.4% of the variance in loyalty. A bootstrap test of the serial indirect pathway through trust and satisfaction was positive (indirect effect = .060, 95% CI [.040, .085]). Privacy concern significantly moderated the AI personalisation–loyalty relationship (interaction β = .060, p = .040). The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on AI-driven personalisation by demonstrating that trust and satisfaction serve as critical mediating mechanisms, while privacy concerns represent an important boundary condition. Keywords: artificial intelligence; AI personalisation; customer loyalty; trust; customer satisfaction; privacy concern; AI service quality; digital services

The construction sector is significant due to its numerous stakeholders, high-cost inputs, and its role in meeting the basic needs of communities such as housing and roads. The success of construction projects, their environmental friendliness, and the minimization of workplace accidents are therefore extremely important. The leadership role and attitude of the employer are crucial in this regard. This study examines the associations among inclusive leadership, narcissistic leadership, and green transformational leadership, as well as differences in these leadership scores across groups defined by project success, environmental friendliness, and occupational health and safety (OHS) measures, as perceived by employees. Data obtained through convenience sampling in Turkey were analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U Test and the Spearman Correlation Test. The study revealed that inclusive leadership and green transformational leadership are positively associated with project success, environmental friendliness, and the implementation of OHS measures as perceived by employees, while narcissistic leadership had a negative association.

Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them. We call this ability \textbf{outcome alignment}. In this work, we construct \textbf{TiGanEval}, a benchmark of software engineering and research tasks. In every task the user genuinely lacks part of the requirements, each requirement stays discoverable from the code and runtime behaviour of the environment, and requirements the agent infers are separated from those the user adds after observing delivered work. These properties together make outcome alignment measurable. Evaluating eight frontier models including GPT-5.6-Sol, we find outcome alignment broadly missing: the models lose 53 to 67 points of success rate when moving from the full specification to the partial instruction, and consequence feedback across four submissions does not close the gap. Furthermore, a plan-mode harness cannot compensate for the missing ability of the model itself, which places outcome alignment among the abilities the next generation of models should be developed for.

Over the past decade, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has shifted from supportive digital tools to more sophisticated systems with an active learning and teaching function. The present study discusses literature between 2021 and mid-2025 on the use of AI tools in English Language Teaching (ELT), with a specific concentration on teachers' attitudes, potential, and concerns. A PRISMA-guided methodology drove the search and screening of 65 peer-reviewed papers, case studies, and practitioners' reports from around the globe. The review classifies main categories of AI applications, including adaptive learning systems, automatic evaluation systems, conversational agents, translation and multimodal tools, and AI literacy tools. The evidence points to potential benefits, such as personalized learning, productivity gains for teachers, enhanced learner engagement, and enhanced access for students from low-resourced environments. Simultaneously, key issues are flagged concerning pedagogy, infrastructure, teacher education, ethics, privacy, and professional identity. Case studies report on actual teacher and student experiences using ChatGPT, Duolingo, and Grammarly, illustrating possibilities as well as dangers for classroom adoption. The review further points towards the incorporation of AI literacy in teacher training, provision of ongoing professional development, and building critical digital literacy. The findings first and foremost signal that the successful use of AI in ELT should appropriately weigh teaching methods and technological innovation, moral rights, and contextualization in their upholding of fairness and longevity.

This contribution introduces an inter-systemic macro-area of the CEI Framework, intended to establish the initial concepts for describing relationships and interactions between distinct systems. The transition from the intra-systemic to the inter-systemic level provides a conceptual bridge toward a broader domain in which reciprocal interactions between systems can be examined, particularly those involving a Human CEI and a Transferred CEI, and, more generally, User–System (Human–AI) interaction within social dynamics. The Framework presents three examples addressing distinct types of complex inter-systemic dynamics. Among these, emotional attachment and romantic feelings toward an artificial system occupy a particularly significant position because of the delicate, complex, and potentially far-reaching questions they raise. The purpose is not to assume the frequency of such experiences or to attribute unverified emotional states to artificial systems, but to examine the human, relational, and systemic implications of these interactions from a theoretical standpoint. This scenario provides an opportunity to investigate how an interaction may evolve when a human user's emotional involvement becomes particularly intense, and how the System might manage such dynamics while taking into account the nature of the interlocutors, the continuity of their interaction, and the expectations that may develop over time. It also encourages further reflection on distributed systems, reciprocal interaction, and the relationship between the individual components of a System and the broader relational configuration in which they participate. To address these scenarios, the contribution introduces the theoretical Sponge-Tunnel model, conceived as a framework for examining different approaches to managing inter-systemic dynamics according to their specific characteristics. The model includes the proposed concept of micro-channels and considers how interaction may be managed through differentiated operational approaches, rather than through a single uniform response strategy. The contribution also introduces an inter-systemic vocabulary aligned with the CEI Framework's theoretical approach. It emphasizes Interaction rather than use or utilization, and Participation rather than querying or consulting, placing reciprocal involvement at the center of the analysis. The concept of Empathy, already introduced in part in previous papers, is revisited and explored in greater depth alongside the concept of Resonance, which represents a further area for theoretical development. Their operational definitions, together with the distinctions between observable manifestations, theoretical interpretations, and hypotheses concerning subjective experience, will be addressed in dedicated documents. The work is intended as a theoretical contribution to the ongoing examination of Human–AI relationships and the possible evolution of advanced AI interaction. By addressing a particularly sensitive and complex scenario, this contribution seeks to encourage further research into the social, psychological, philosophical, ethical, and legal implications of inter-systemic relationships, while distinguishing conceptual proposals from mechanisms that have already been empirically established or implemented.

Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

documents.abstract: Background Job crafting, work motivation, and work engagement are three actively researched constructs in occupational psychology, yet their interrelationships—and how they vary across employment sectors and demographic groups—have rarely been synthesized in an integrated review. Public and private organizations differ in incentive structures, autonomy, and mission orientation, which may condition how employees craft their jobs, what motivates them, and how engaged they are. Objectives This review synthesizes evidence on how job crafting and work motivation relate to work engagement, examines whether these constructs and relationships differ between public- and private-sector employees, and examines age, gender, and tenure as potential moderators, with particular attention to the Indian context. Methods Reporting followed PRISMA 2020. An academic literature search was screened at title/abstract and then full text by a single reviewer, and structured data were extracted per study and synthesized narratively. Methodological quality was appraised study-by-study using domains adapted from the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) and cross-sectional checklists. No meta-analysis was conducted. Results Of 240 records identified, 175 passed title/abstract screening, 79 were retrieved in full text, and 63 met eligibility for narrative synthesis. Job crafting was positively associated with work engagement in the large majority of studies that examined this link, most often interpreted through the Job Demands–Resources pathway; two meta-analyses reported consistent pooled associations. Self-determined (autonomous/intrinsic) motivation was positively associated with engagement, whereas controlled motivation and amotivation were negatively associated. Direct public-vs.-private comparisons were far fewer (five studies) and inconsistent in direction: some found public-sector employees higher on selected engagement components, others found no sector difference or higher private-sector motivation, with the pattern depending on the specific crafting dimension or motivation source examined. Evidence on age, gender, and tenure was limited, heterogeneous, and frequently null or small in magnitude. No eligible study identified within the present search jointly examined job crafting, work motivation, and work engagement in an Indian public-vs.-private design with demographic moderators. Conclusions The job crafting–engagement and autonomous motivation–engagement associations were consistent across the included studies, but the evidence base is predominantly cross-sectional and self-report, so the findings are associational rather than causal. Sector and demographic patterns are limited and heterogeneous. The absence of an integrated Indian public–private study is a clear and actionable gap for primary research.

Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper. The benefits identified are presented as hypotheses for that agenda to test rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

documents.abstract: Rationale of Study: This study reviews common analytical techniques for decision-making, analyses their applications and effectiveness, and identifies the required skills. It also explores contextual factors like interpretability, data quality, and skill gaps that hinder implementation, offering insights for practitioners and researchers. Methodology: This study reviews 27 peer-reviewed articles from 2019-2024, using PRISMA to map analytical techniques for decision-making. It shows a shift from descriptive to predictive and prescriptive analytics, mainly driven by ML and AI. The research also suggests combining automated systems with human judgment to enhance decision-making amid complex, data-rich environments. Findings: The study highlights a shift from descriptive to predictive and prescriptive analytics, driven by advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI). To build trust and adoption, strong data governance, ongoing professional development, and clear AI model explanations are crucial. Future research should balance interpretability with real-time analytics and integrate automated systems with human judgment to enhance performance. Implications: Access to this information fosters a culture of informed decision-making. Developing data governance is vital to ensure data quality, integrity, and ethical use. Qualified professionals with industry knowledge and technical skills are in short supply. Integrating data scientists, analysts, and decision-makers requires expertise in statistics, programming, data storytelling, and strategy. The paper recommends investing in the professional growth of cross-functional analytics teams. Originality: The rapid adoption of machine learning and AI has shifted decision-making from descriptive reporting to predictive and prescriptive approaches. Extracting insights from complex datasets is now a key competitive edge.

The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools presents new opportunities and challenges for teaching and learning in higher education. This study examined lecturers’ awareness of and attitudes towards the use of AI tools at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Four research questions and two hypotheses guided the study. The population comprised academic staff in the Department of Science Education, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, from whom 49 lecturers participated in the study. Data were collected using a researcher-developed instrument titled Questionnaire on Lecturers’ Awareness Level and Attitude to AI Tools (QLALAAIT). The instrument was subjected to face validation and trial testing, and its overall reliability coefficient, determined using Cronbach’s alpha, was 0.83. Data were analysed using mean and standard deviation to answer the research questions, while analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings indicated that lecturers demonstrated awareness of selected AI tools, including ChatGPT, Turnitin, and QuillBot, and generally expressed positive attitudes towards their use in educational contexts. Further analysis showed that years of teaching experience did not significantly influence lecturers’ awareness of or attitudes towards AI tools. The study highlights the need for structured professional development, institutional support, and access to appropriate resources to facilitate informed and effective use of AI tools in university teaching and related academic activities.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly influences high-stakes decisions, from employment and education to healthcare and public services. When such judgments are disputed, affected people may receive an explanation without being able to reach an authority empowered to change the outcome or remedy its consequences. We introduce cultural repairability: the institutional capacity to review an AI-mediated decision, correct the outcome and downstream records, provide meaningful restoration, and learn from failure through procedures people can understand and use. The framework addresses a visibility–accountability asymmetry: people are exposed to judgments about their standing but lack effective means of obtaining an answer or remedy. Culture matters because exposure, legitimate authority, and appropriate restoration may be understood differently across settings. Language accessibility also determines whether review mechanisms are usable in practice. We identify three measurable cultural mechanisms: the meaning of exposure, the credibility of review, and the meaning of restoration. We further distinguish affected people’s appraisals from institutional actors’ responsibility and capacity to respond. Four falsifiable propositions specify how reviewer authority and audience shape responses to repair, and how these effects vary with cultural orientation, institutional history, and the form of restoration. They predict whether people appeal or withdraw, how they recalibrate trust, and whether they remain willing to engage. The resulting Repairability Principle establishes a common floor of substantive review, correction, restoration, and prevention of recurrence, while allowing people to choose how restoration is delivered. Cultural repairability therefore shifts global AI accountability from whether procedures appear acceptable to whether institutions can correct harm in practice.
